paragraphs: Swamiji was a big fan of Alice in Wonderland. He called it the most wonderful children's book of his century and said that reading it had delighted him; he had always wanted to write something like it for children himself.

What he loved most was the very thing adults find strange about it: nothing is connected. One idea jumps into the next with no logic at all. Yet when we were children, Swamiji pointed out, such leaps felt perfectly sensible. The author had simply gone back to the way he thought as a child and written from there. By contrast, books that try to force grown-up ideas on children are, in his view, nonsense. We adults, he joked, are only grown-up children.

Then he turned the book into a lesson about life. The world, he said, is just as unconnected as Wonderland. When we see things happen in a certain order often enough, we label it cause and effect and expect it to repeat. In a dream, too, everything seems to fit together perfectly; only on waking do we notice how little sense it made.

In the same way, when we wake up from this dream of the world and compare it with Reality, it will look like a parade of nonsense passing before us. We do not know where it comes from or where it goes, only that it will end. That, said Swamiji, is Maya, as fleeting as drifting clouds.
learn: The patterns and rules we take for granted may be less solid than they seem. Hold your assumptions lightly, keep a childlike curiosity, and stay open to the idea that there is a deeper reality behind the everyday show.
